clinicalPearls: Characterised by excessive eccrine sweating beyond physiological needs, focal and symmetrical, most often affecting the palms, soles, axillae and craniofacial skin
Onset is usually in childhood or adolescence, and there is frequently a positive family history
By definition the excess sweating stops during sleep, a key feature distinguishing it from secondary generalised hyperhidrosis
It can cause considerable social, occupational and psychological impairment despite being a benign condition
The eccrine glands are structurally normal, and the problem lies in their neural overstimulation rather than in gland pathology
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by criteria such as focal symmetrical sweating for at least six months, early onset, family history and cessation during sleep
Complications include maceration, secondary bacterial and fungal infection, pitted keratolysis and contact dermatitis

Treatment follows a stepwise approach with topical antiperspirants (aluminium salts), iontophoresis for palms and soles, botulinum toxin injections for focal areas, and systemic anticholinergics or surgery in resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: Primary focal hyperhidrosis is thought to result from an exaggerated or dysregulated sympathetic response producing excessive cholinergic stimulation of structurally normal eccrine sweat glands. The eccrine glands are innervated by sympathetic fibres that release acetylcholine, and in affected individuals these glands are overstimulated out of proportion to thermoregulatory need, particularly at sites of high eccrine density such as the palms, soles and axillae. The frequent family history suggests a genetic predisposition, and emotional and thermal stimuli often exacerbate the sweating. The cessation of symptoms during sleep reflects the withdrawal of the emotional and cortical drive to sympathetic outflow.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary generalised hyperhidrosis from systemic disease (thyrotoxicosis, diabetes, phaeochromocytoma)
Menopausal or hormonally driven sweating and flushing
Anxiety and other psychiatric causes of sweating
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment against diagnostic criteria including symmetry, early onset and cessation during sleep
Focused history and examination to exclude features of secondary hyperhidrosis
Thyroid function tests and glucose when a systemic cause is suspected
Gravimetric or starch-iodine testing to map and quantify affected areas when required
Assessment for secondary skin infection such as pitted keratolysis or dermatophytosis
Screening for phaeochromocytoma or other endocrine causes if the pattern is generalised or nocturnal
redFlags: Generalised, asymmetrical or night-time sweating suggesting a secondary systemic cause
Associated weight loss, fever or lymphadenopathy pointing to infection or malignancy
Unilateral sweating raising concern about underlying neurological or thoracic pathology
Sudden onset in adulthood without a lifelong history
reference.prognosis: Primary focal hyperhidrosis is a benign, chronic condition that often persists for many years but frequently improves with age; quality of life can be substantially restored with appropriate stepwise treatment, and it carries no threat to general health.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish primary focal from secondary generalised hyperhidrosis and missing an underlying systemic cause
Underestimating the psychosocial burden of a benign condition
Escalating to invasive treatment before trialling topical antiperspirants and iontophoresis
Overlooking secondary skin infection such as pitted keratolysis
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on hyperhidrosis
management: Stepwise first-line topical aluminium chloride hexahydrate antiperspirant applied to the affected sites
Tap-water iontophoresis for palmar and plantar disease
Intradermal botulinum toxin injections for axillary or palmar hyperhidrosis unresponsive to topical measures
Topical or oral anticholinergic agents such as glycopyrronium or oxybutynin for craniofacial or more widespread sweating, counselling on dry mouth and other antimuscarinic effects

Energy-based axillary treatment such as microwave thermolysis or local gland excision, reserving endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy for severe refractory palmar disease with explicit warning about compensatory sweating
Treat coexisting skin complications such as pitted keratolysis or dermatophyte infection
Address the psychological, social and occupational impact and reassure regarding the benign nature
Reassess and exclude a secondary cause if sweating becomes generalised, nocturnal or of late onset
